entries.definition: The science of planting and growing trees in forests.
entries.example: She studied forestry and environmental management.

entries.definition: The woody part of a tree arising from the trunk and usually dividing.
entries.example: Selfe loue, to him ſelf tender, to the reſt tough, / Is, of iuſt iuſtice, neither roote, braunce, nor bough. / Loue (namely ſelfe loue) corruptibly growyng, / Is cheefe lodeſter of lets, in iuſtice ſhowing.

entries.definition: A projecting body part, especially an elephant's long nose, or the central body excluding the head and limbs.
entries.example: The elephant curled its trunk around a branch.

entries.definition: A tree-branch, usually a primary one directly attached to the trunk.
entries.example: When the bough breaks, the cradle will fall. (Rock-a-bye Baby)

entries.definition: The part of a plant, generally underground, that anchors and supports the plant body, absorbs and stores water and nutrients, and in some plants is able to perform vegetative reproduction.
entries.example: This tree's roots can go as deep as twenty metres underground.

entries.definition: Grass cut and dried for use as animal fodder.
entries.example: Make hay while sunne shines.

entries.definition: A dried stalk of a cereal plant.
entries.example: A single straw caught in the horse's mane.

entries.definition: Any of various types of tall stiff perennial grass-like plants growing together in groups near water.
entries.example: A reed grew beside the edge of the pond.

entries.definition: A modified branch that is hard and sharp like a spike.
entries.example: A sharp thorn scratched my hand as I picked the rose.

entries.definition: Any plant unwanted at the place where and at the time when it is growing.
entries.example: If it isn't in a straight line or marked with a label, it's a weed.

entries.definition: Any plant of the family Poaceae, characterized by leaves that arise from nodes in the stem and leaf bases that wrap around the stem, especially those grown as ground cover rather than for grain.
entries.example: Thou turnest man to destruction: and sayest, Returne yee children of men. / For a thousand yeeres in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past: and as a watch in the night. / Thou carriest them away as with a flood, they are as a sleepe: in the morning they are like grasse which groweth vp. / In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth vp: in the euening it is cut downe, and withereth.

entries.definition: A field or pasture; a piece of land either intentionally cultivated with grass or (especially) naturally covered with grass, especially one that is intended to be mown for hay or to be grazed.
entries.example: alpine meadows

entries.definition: Ground (generally in front of or around a house) covered with grass kept closely mown.
entries.example: Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path[…]. It twisted and turned,[…]and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn. And, back of the lawn, was a big, old-fashioned house, with piazzas stretching in front of it, and all blazing with lights. 'Twas the house I'd seen the roof of from the beach.

entries.definition: A small oval fruit eaten after curing and also used to produce oil.
entries.example: She added a green olive to the salad.
entries.usage: Selected the edible fruit rather than the tree.

entries.definition: Any coniferous tree of the genus Pinus.
entries.example: The northern slopes were covered mainly in pine.

entries.definition: Any plant whose stem requires support and which climbs by tendrils or twining.
entries.example: The vine climbed up the wooden trellis.

entries.definition: A plant or flower of the genus Viola, especially the fragrant Viola odorata; (inexact) similar-looking plants and flowers.
entries.example: Refreshed by their cooling bath of evening dew, the violets and other nocturnal flowers emitted a pleasant fragrance over the fields, but from the bogs and the rivulets came up now and then damp, penetrating gusts, that sent an icy chill through me.

entries.definition: A type of flowering plant, genus Tulipa.
entries.example: "The sturdy burghers of Holland took the tulip mania so badly that single bulbs that could not flower till another year would sell for more than $2000 apiece."

entries.definition: A building or institution where money (originally, only coins) is produced under government licence.
entries.example: The mint produced thousands of new coins.

entries.definition: A chain or range of rocks, sand, or coral lying at or near the surface of the water.
entries.example: The boat slowed as it approached the shallow reef.

entries.definition: Any of many aquatic photosynthetic organisms, including the seaweeds, whose size ranges from a single cell to giant kelps and whose biochemistry and forms are very diverse, some being eukaryotic.
entries.example: For example, the antitumour depsipeptide kahalalide F was isolated from the opisthobranch mollusc Elysia rufescens, and is used by both the mollusc and its dietary alga Bryopsis spp.

entries.definition: A biomolecule that catalyses a biological chemical reaction: either a globular protein with this function or an RNA molecule with this function.
entries.example: The enzyme helps break down starch during digestion.

entries.definition: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process.
entries.example: Enzymes, the catalysts of biological systems, are remarkable molecular devices that determine the pattern of chemical transformations.

entries.definition: The event of setting (someone or something) free (e.g. hostages, slaves, prisoners, caged animals, hooked or stuck mechanisms).
entries.example: Similar studies of rats have employed four different intracranial resorbable, slow sustained release systems—surgical foam, a thermal gel depot, a microcapsule or biodegradable polymer beads.

entries.definition: The release of a substance such as gas into the environment.
entries.example: The factory reduced its carbon emissions by installing new equipment.
entries.usage: Typical combinations: carbon emissions, reduce emissions, emission target.

entries.definition: To include so that it no longer has separate existence; to overwhelm; to cause to disappear as if by swallowing up; to incorporate; to assimilate; to take in and use up.
entries.example: Dark oblivion soon absorbs them all.

entries.definition: The act of moving in a circle, or in a course which brings the moving body to the place where its motion began.
entries.example: Exercise can improve blood circulation.

entries.definition: To be larger, greater than (something).
entries.example: The company's 2005 revenue exceeds that of 2004.

entries.definition: Understanding or comprehension.
entries.example: He was quick on the uptake and understood the instructions immediately.
entries.usage: Often used in quick or slow on the uptake.

entries.definition: A source of nourishment, such as food, that can be metabolized by an organism to give energy and build tissue.
entries.example: Even second-generation biofuels, made from crop wastes or wood, are an environmental disaster, either extending the cultivated area or removing the straw and stovers which protect the soil from erosion and keep carbon and nutrients in the ground.

entries.definition: The impetus behind all motion and all activity.
entries.example: A “moving platform” scheme[…]is more technologically ambitious than maglev trains even though it relies on conventional rails.[…]This set-up solves several problems […]. Stopping high-speed trains wastes energy and time, so why not simply slow them down enough for a moving platform to pull alongside?

entries.definition: The places, conditions and objects around someone or something.
entries.example: The quiet surroundings made the cottage a good place to study.

entries.definition: Any mechanical means for the conversion or control of motion, or the transmission or control of power.
entries.example: A spring mechanism closes the door automatically.

entries.definition: A weight that is put in opposition to an equal weight so it keeps that in balance.
entries.example: A heavy counterbalance keeps the crane stable while it lifts the load.

entries.definition: To keep safe; to defend; to guard; to prevent harm coming to.
entries.example: to protect a child from danger

entries.definition: To protect something and keep it from harm or damage.
entries.example: The museum controls humidity to preserve old manuscripts.

entries.definition: Protection of the natural environment or careful use of resources.
entries.example: The charity supports the conservation of coastal habitats.
entries.usage: Typical combinations: wildlife conservation, energy conservation, conservation programme.

entries.definition: Alternative form of bushfire.
entries.example: Australia has always been prone to bush fires due to its woody landscape.

entries.definition: Bring something, especially a fire or flame, to an end.
entries.example: The firefighters managed to extinguish the flames.

entries.definition: To destroy itself, usually by a built-in mechanism.
entries.example: The device is programmed to destruct if its security seal is broken.
entries.usage: This is an uncommon technical verb; self-destruct is the conventional general form. The self-destruction sense replaces the nonstandard transitive default.

entries.definition: The remains of a destroyed or dilapidated construction, such as a house or castle.
entries.example: The Veian and the Gabian towirs shall fall, / And one promiscuous ruin cover all; / Nor, after length of years, a stone betray / The place where once the very ruins lay.

entries.definition: To decay and disappear; to waste away to nothing.
entries.example:
1881, Tarafa, translated by W. A. Clouston, The Poem of Tarafa
I consider time as a treasure decreasing every night; and that which every day diminishes soon perishes for ever.

entries.definition: To destroy (buildings, etc.), especially in a planned or intentional fashion.
entries.example: They demolished the old mill and put up four townhouses.

entries.definition: To break or violate a treaty, a law, a right, etc.
entries.example: Near-synonyms: flout, infract

entries.definition: To dig underneath (something), to make a passage for destructive or military purposes; to sap.
entries.example: Martin, for instance, had on one occasion undermined a tree sacred to old gods, then stood in the path of its fall, but forced it to fall elsewhere by making the sign of the Cross.

entries.definition: The action of making or becoming extinct; annihilation.
entries.example: Thirteen long centuries have elapsed since the extinction of the last Zoroastrian Empire[…]

entries.definition: Model, example.
entries.example: The wallpaper had a floral pattern.

entries.definition: That which is produced or occurs as a result of an event or process.
entries.example: A quality automobile is the outcome of the work of skilled engineers and thousands of workers.

entries.definition: The striking of one body against another; collision.
entries.example: The helmet protected his head from the impact.

entries.definition: Of, related to, or reliant on a season or period of the year, especially with regard to weather characteristics.
entries.example: It is a seasonal swimming pool.

entries.definition: Pertaining to or founded on experiment.
entries.example: Chemistry is an experimental science.

entries.definition: Apt to win favour; pleasing.
entries.example: The candidate wearing the business suit made a favourable impression.

entries.definition: Capable of producing something, especially in abundance; fertile.
entries.example: The fertile soil made the farm highly productive.

entries.definition: Having the power to produce a required effect or effects.
entries.example: The pill is an effective method of birth control.

entries.definition: Making good, thorough, or careful use of resources; not consuming extra. Especially, making good use of time or energy.
entries.example: An efficient process would automate all the routine work.

entries.definition: Large in amount or degree.
entries.example: The project requires considerable investment.

entries.definition: Very large in size or extent.
entries.example: Compared to its counterparts from World War II, the Abrams main battle tank is truly massive.

entries.definition: Huge, gigantic, very large.
entries.example: Then everybody once more knelt, and soon the blessing was pronounced. The choir and the clergy trooped out slowly, […], down the nave to the western door. […] At a seemingly immense distance the surpliced group stopped to say the last prayer.

entries.definition: Largest, greatest (in magnitude), highest, most.
entries.example: The organification of iodide in the thyroid gland was described using a second order rate constant (KthybindC, /nmol/L*hr/kg thyroid weight) fitted to provide thyroidal iodide stores near the maximal value, which increased with age.

entries.definition: The smallest possible amount, quantity, or degree.
entries.example: With minimal effort, you won't be able to achieve all your dreams.

entries.definition: The best, most favourable or desirable, especially under some restriction.
entries.example: Finding the optimal balance between features and price is a common problem.

entries.definition: A student or professor of biology; one versed in the science of biology.
entries.example: Not long ago, it was difficult to produce photographs of tiny creatures with every part in focus.[…]A photo processing technique called focus stacking has changed that. Developed as a tool to electronically combine the sharpest bits of multiple digital images, focus stacking is a boon to biologists seeking full focus on a micron scale.

entries.definition: One who studies or practices zoology.
entries.example: The zoologist observed how the monkeys shared food.

entries.definition: A scholar of ecology.
entries.example: Planting trees to combat climate change is a waste of time, according to a study by ecologists who say that most forests do not have any overall effect on global temperature, while those furthest from the equator could actually be making global warming worse.

entries.definition: A person engaged in botany, the scientific study of plants.
entries.example: It is probably the Livistona rotundifolia of botanists, and is the most complete and beautiful fan-leaf I have ever seen, serving admirably for folding into water-buckets and impromptu baskets, as well as for thatching and other purposes.

entries.definition: A vertebrate animal of the class Mammalia, characterized by being warm-blooded, having fur or hair and producing milk with which to feed their young.
entries.example: A whale is a mammal, even though it lives in water.

entries.definition: A mammal of the order Primates, comprising of apes (including humans), monkeys, lemurs, tarsiers, lorisids, and galagos.
entries.example: Primates range from lemurs to gorillas.

entries.definition: Having a backbone.
entries.example: Fish are vertebrate animals because they have backbones.

entries.definition: A (typically scaly and egg-laying) cold-blooded vertebrate tetrapod animal, of the class Reptilia (excluding birds), such as a lizard, turtle, snake, crocodile, alligator, etc.
entries.example: A snake is a reptile, as are lizards and crocodiles.

entries.definition: An animal such as a frog or salamander, typically living both in water and on land during its life.
entries.example: A frog is an amphibian.

entries.definition: An organism that feeds chiefly on animals; an animal that feeds on meat as the main part of its diet.
entries.example: As juveniles the crocodiles are frequently predated by larger carnivores.

entries.definition: An organism that feeds chiefly on plants; an animal that feeds on herbage or vegetation as the main part of its diet.
entries.example: It is unlikely that any member of the hominin clade was either an obligate herbivore or an obligate carnivore

entries.definition: A living being, such as an animal, monster, or alien.
entries.example: insects and other creatures

entries.definition: undomesticated animals, especially mammals, birds, and fish, which live in the wild.
entries.example: This town offers wildlife tours where you can go and watch the bears, deer, wild rabbits and other creatures in their natural habitats.

entries.definition: Animals considered as a group; especially those of a particular country, region, time, biological group, etc.
entries.example: the flora and fauna

entries.definition: Plants considered as a group, especially those of a particular country, region, time, etc.
entries.example: Thirdly, I continue to attempt to interdigitate the taxa in our flora with taxa of the remainder of the world.

entries.definition: A group of organisms that share characteristics and can reproduce together.
entries.example: Several bird species return to the lake each spring.
entries.usage: Typical combinations: endangered species, native species, protect a species.

entries.definition: A number of birds together in a group, such as those gathered together for the purpose of migration.
entries.example: He told his father, and said it would be just suitable work for him to run about fields and woods amongst the strawberry hills after a flock of hares, and now and then lie down and take a nap on some sunny hill.

entries.definition: A number of domestic animals assembled together under the watch or ownership of a keeper.
entries.example: a herd of cattle

entries.definition: A large number of insects or other bugs (e.g. centipedes), especially when in motion or (for bees) migrating to a new colony.
entries.example: […] reſtleſs thoughts, that like a deadly ſwarm / Of Hornets arm'd […] ruſh upon me thronging,

entries.definition: A group of people crowded or gathered closely together.
entries.example:
Not to know me argues yourselves unknown,
The lowest of your throng.

entries.definition: To press forward; to advance by pushing.
entries.example: The man crowded into the packed room.

entries.definition: Any four-footed land mammal.
entries.example: Whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is clovenfooted, and cheweth the cud, among the beasts, that shall ye eat.

entries.definition: Without reason or intelligence (of animals).
entries.example: a brute beast

entries.definition: Intentionally causing or reveling in pain and suffering; merciless, heartless.
entries.example: The supervisor was very cruel to Josh, as he would always give Josh the hardest, most degrading work he could find.

entries.definition: To obtain or receive (something) from something else.
entries.example: Reading books is the best way to derive knowledge.

entries.definition: To cause (someone or something) to be; to bring (someone or something) into existence; to produce or initiate a person or thing.
entries.example: Einstein originated the theory of relativity.

entries.definition: The stock of a family; a race or generation of progenitors.
entries.example: Where ye may all that are of noble ſtemm / Approach, and kiſs her ſacred veſtures hemm.

entries.definition: One from whom a person is descended, whether on the father's or mother's side, at any distance of time; a progenitor; a forefather; a forebear.
entries.example: Whether modern, industrial man is less or more warlike than his hunter-gatherer ancestors is impossible to determine. The machine gun is so much more lethal than the bow and arrow that comparisons are meaningless.

entries.definition: Descending; going down.
entries.example: The elevator resumed its descendant trajectory.

entries.definition: A person's daughter or son; a person's child.
entries.example: We are the offspring of Italian immigrants.

entries.definition: A group within a larger group; a group whose members are some, but not all, of the members of a larger group.
entries.example:
1998, Robert A. Johnson, Prevalence of Substance Use Among Racial and Ethnic Subgroups in the United States, 1991-1993, Department of Health and Human Services, page B-11,
Based on U.S. Bureau of the Census (1992c), other metropolitan areas that might be suitable for oversampling specific racial/ethnic subgroups include Miami (18% Cuban), New York City (7% Puerto Rican), Los Angeles (26% Mexican), and Honolulu (23% Japanese). Three techniques might be used to increase the yield of rare subgroup members within metropolitan areas where they are concentrated: 1) oversampling of areal segments containing high percentages of the subgroup, […] .

entries.definition: To give (someone or something) food to eat.
entries.example: Feed the dog every evening.

entries.definition: To produce offspring sexually; to bear young.
entries.example: Plant breeding is always a numbers game.[…]The wild species we use are rich in genetic variation, and individual plants are highly heterozygous and do not breed true. In addition, we are looking for rare alleles, so the more plants we try, the better.

entries.definition: To breed or reproduce within an isolated community.
entries.example: The isolated animals could only interbreed within their small population.

entries.definition: To cross different varieties or species to produce hybrids.
entries.example: The researchers hybridise two varieties of wheat to produce a new strain.

entries.definition: To increase in number or spread rapidly; to multiply.
entries.example: The flowers proliferated rapidly all spring.

entries.definition: The state or quality of being sterile.
entries.example: The team tested the sterility of the surgical equipment.

entries.definition: A fellow, comrade, colleague, partner or someone with whom something is shared, e.g. shipmate, classmate.
entries.example: A "mate" was a "mate" - share and share alike, no matter how bad might be the times, or how long a spell of ill luck had attended them.

entries.definition: Behaviour by an animal that attracts a mate before mating.
entries.example: The birds perform an elaborate courtship dance.

entries.definition: To place down in a position of rest, or in a horizontal position.
entries.example: to lay a book on the table; to lay a body in the grave

entries.definition: A horizontal door in a floor or ceiling.
entries.example: Moving the wardrobe revealed a previously hidden hatch in the ground.

entries.definition: The young of certain animals, especially a group of young birds or fowl hatched at one time by the same mother.
entries.example: As a hen doth gather her brood under her wings.

entries.definition: To produce or deposit (eggs) in water.
entries.example: A frog spawns thousands of tadpoles every year.

entries.definition: Fully developed; grown up in terms of physical appearance, behaviour or thinking; ripe.
entries.example: She is quite mature for her age.

entries.definition: The outer protective layer of the body of any animal, including of a human.
entries.example: He is so disgusting he makes my skin crawl.

entries.definition: A curved, pointed, horny projection on each digit of the foot of a mammal, reptile, or bird.
entries.example: The cat caught its claw on the curtain.

entries.definition: The soft foot of a mammal or other animal, generally a quadruped, that has claws or nails; comparable to a human hand or foot.
entries.example: The cat injured its paw on a piece of broken glass.

entries.definition: A rigid structure projecting from the front of a bird's face, used for pecking, grooming, foraging, carrying items, eating food, etc.
entries.example: The bird used its beak to pick up seeds.

entries.definition: One of the appendages of a fish, used to propel itself and to manoeuvre/maneuver.
entries.example: The fish's fins minimize water flow.

entries.definition: An appendage of an animal's (bird, bat, insect) body that enables it to fly.
entries.example: The bird was flapping its wings

entries.definition: A token of honour or prowess; that on which one prides oneself; a prize or reward.
entries.example: But well thou comſt / Before thy fellows, ambitious to win / From me ſom Plume, that thy ſucceſs may ſhow / Deſtruction to the reſt: […]

entries.definition: A branching, hair-like structure that grows on the bodies of birds, used for flight, swimming, protection and display.
entries.example: Notice, too, that the shaft is not straight, but bent so that the upper surface of the feather is convex, and the lower concave.

entries.definition: The hairy coat of various mammal species, especially when fine, soft and thick.
entries.example: The fox's thick fur kept it warm in winter.

entries.definition: A stiff or coarse hair on a nonhuman mammal or on a plant.
entries.example: the bristles of a pig

entries.definition: A curving piece or lock of hair; a ringlet.
entries.example: My hair doesn't have much curl.

entries.definition: An arthropod (in the Insecta class) characterized by six legs, up to four wings, and a chitinous exoskeleton.
entries.example: Our shed has several insect infestations, including ants, yellowjackets, and wasps.

entries.definition: A generally tubular invertebrate of the annelid phylum; an earthworm.
entries.example: ‘Children crawled over each other like little grey worms in the gutters,’ he said. ‘The only red things about them were their buttocks and they were raw. Their faces looked as if snails had slimed on them and their mothers were like great sick beasts whose byres had never been cleared.[…]’

entries.definition: Any destructive insect that attacks crops or livestock; an agricultural pest.
entries.example: This insect is a pest that damages young fruit trees.

entries.definition: An organism that lives on or in another organism of a different species, deriving benefit from living on or in that other organism, while not contributing towards that other organism sufficiently to cover the cost to that other organism.
entries.example: Lice, fleas, ticks, and mites are widely spread parasites.

entries.definition: Any of various eight-legged, predatory arthropods, of the order Araneae, most of which spin webs to catch prey.
entries.example: Little Miss Muffet, She sat on a tuffet, Eating of curds and whey; There came a little spider, Who sat down beside her, And frighted Miss Muffet away.

entries.definition: A flying insect of the order Lepidoptera, distinguished from moths by their diurnal activity and generally brighter colouring.
entries.example: It is true. I am like a butterfly, and I shall only live a little while.

entries.definition: A small flying insect of the family Culicidae, the females of which bite humans and animals and suck blood, leaving an itching bump on the skin, and sometimes carrying diseases like malaria, dengue and yellow fever.
entries.example: I do not quite know what it was that made me poke my head out of the friendly shelter of the blanket, perhaps because I found that the mosquitoes were biting right through it.

entries.definition: An insect known for the chirping sound made by rubbing its forewings together.
entries.example: A cricket chirped somewhere in the grass.

entries.definition: Any of several flightless sea birds, of the family Spheniscidae within the order Sphenisciformes, found in the Southern Hemisphere, marked by their usual upright stance, walking on short legs, and (generally) their stark black and white plumage.
entries.example: Here are also birds cal'd Pen-gwins (white-head in Welch) like Pigmies walking upright, their finns or wings hanging very orderly downe like sleeves […]

entries.definition: A pinniped (Pinnipedia), particularly an earless seal (true seal) or eared seal.
entries.example: The seals in the harbor looked better than they smelled.

entries.definition: Any of various land-dwelling reptiles, of the family Testudinidae (chiefly Canada, US) or the order Testudines (chiefly UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, South Africa, India), whose body is enclosed in a shell (carapace plus plastron). The animal can withdraw its head and four legs partially into the shell, providing some protection from predators.
entries.example: The tortoise, with its characteristic protrusion of the head and neck, was a symbol sacred to Venus. It represented the procreative principle.

entries.definition: Any land, aquatic, or semi-aquatic reptile of the order Testudines, characterised by a protective shell enclosing its body. See also tortoise.
entries.example: A unique anti-aphrodisiac was the heart of a turtle carried in a wolf's skin. It prevented a person from ever being tempted amorously.

entries.definition: Any large cetacean, usually with the exclusion of dolphins and porpoises.
entries.example: Near-synonym: baleen (obsolete sense)

entries.definition: A member of the Macropodidae family of large marsupials with strong hind legs for hopping, native to Australia and New Guinea.
entries.example: Besides the Animals which I have before mentioned, called by the Natives Kangooroo, or Kanguru […].

entries.definition: A mammalian beast of burden, much used in desert areas, of the genus Camelus.
entries.example:
Returne our Mules and emptie Camels backe,
That we may trauell into Siria, […]

entries.definition: A large black-and-white bear native to China that feeds mainly on bamboo.
entries.example: The panda ate bamboo beside its cub.
entries.usage: abbreviation, also, alt-of, attributive, colloquial, ellipsis

entries.definition: A large mammal of the family Elephantidae in the order Proboscidea, having a trunk, and native to Africa and Asia.
entries.example: [A] puiſſant olyphant being brought to the place, the grehound ſeming to reioice at the greatnes of the beaſt, rouſed him, and after two or three queſtynges, he lept to the great Olyphante, and after a longe fight ouerthrew hym and kylled hym. So I doubt not but that ſome men […] whiche beeyng ones called to aucthoritee, ioygned with libertee, will inforce theim ſelfes to make theyr miniſtracions noble and excellent.

entries.definition: The hard white form of dentin which forms the tusks of elephants, walruses and other animals.
entries.example: “Leave the ivory!” he cried. “Leave the ivory! Dead men have no use for ivory!” Some of the Manyuema started to lay down their loads, but this was altogether too much for the avaricious Arabs.

entries.definition: A hard growth of keratin that protrudes from the top of the head of certain animals, usually paired.
entries.example: The goat caught one horn in the fence.

entries.definition: A large, generally omnivorous mammal (a few species are purely carnivorous or herbivorous) of the family Ursidae; having shaggy fur, a very small tail, and flat feet.
entries.example: A bear emerged from the forest beside the lake.

entries.definition: Canis lupus; the largest wild member of the canine subfamily.
entries.example: He would listen quietly at meetings of the Politburo, or to distinguished visitors, puffing at his Dunhill pipe, doodling aimlessly - his secretaries Poskrebyshev and Dvinsky write that his pads were sometimes covered with the phrase ‘Lenin-teacher-friend’, but the last foreigner to visit him, in February 1953, noted that he was doodling wolves.

entries.definition: A mythical reptilian or serpentine creature.
entries.example: Medea for the loue of Iaſon, taught him how to tame the fire breathing braſſ feeted Bulls, and kill the mighty dragon that kept the golden fleece[.]

entries.definition: A small wild mammal with pointed ears, a narrow face and a bushy tail.
entries.example: A fox crossed the field at dusk.

entries.definition: A young bear, lion, fox, or similar mammal.
entries.example: The bear cub followed its mother through the trees.
entries.usage: Common learner sense selected in place of an unsuitable or less useful source default.

entries.definition: A young cow or bull of any bovid, such as domestic cattle or buffalo.
entries.example: And Goldenhorns calved. A great day in the wilderness, a joy and a delight. They gave her flour-wash, and Isak himself saw to it there was no stint of flour, though he had carried it all the way himself, on his back. And there lay a pretty calf, a beauty, red-flanked like her mother, and comically bewildered at the miracle of coming into the world. In a couple of years she would be having calves of her own.

entries.definition: A young dog, wolf, fox, seal, bat or shark, or the young of certain other animals.
entries.example: The dog has had that bed since he was just a pup.

entries.definition: A young sheep; especially, one younger than nine months.
entries.example: Mary had a little lamb, its fleece as white as snow.

entries.definition: Domesticated animals of the species Bos taurus (cows, bulls, steers, oxen etc), and other hoofed mammals of the genus Bos.
entries.example: Many cattle were suffering from a disease called BSE.

entries.definition: An adult castrated male of cattle (B. taurus), especially when used as a beast of burden.
entries.example: a yoke of oxen

entries.definition: An adult male bovine, such as a male cow.
entries.example: The farmer kept a bull in a separate field.

entries.definition: An animal from the subtribe Bubalina, also known as true buffalos, such as the Cape buffalo, Syncerus caffer, or the water buffalo, Bubalus bubalis.
entries.example: "It must be a very wild stretch of country, and full of big game. I have always wanted to kill a buffalo before I die."

entries.definition: A hoofed mammal, Equus ferus caballus, often used throughout history for riding and draft work.
entries.example: A cowboy's greatest friend is his horse.

entries.definition: Any of three species of subgenus Hippotigris: Equus grevyi, Equus quagga, or Equus zebra, all with black and white stripes and native to Africa.
entries.example: A group of zebras can be called a dazzle.

entries.definition: A domestic animal, Equus asinus asinus, similar to a horse.
entries.example: Lost last Saturday between twenty and thirty shillings they that have found it please to leave it heare there is five shillings reward by Wm. Roberts that goeth with a Donkey with many thanks

entries.definition: A seat for a rider, typically made of leather and raised in the front and rear, placed on the back of a horse or other animal, and secured by a strap around the animal's body.
entries.example: His [Cotton's] Horſe vvas led before, vvith a mourning Veluet Saddle on his backe, his Coffin had a Crimſon Sattin Quilt lined with purple Silke, ouer him vvas laid his Bible, Svvord and Hat: […]

entries.definition: A restraint or support, especially one consisting of a loop or network of rope or straps, and especially one worn by a working animal such as a horse pulling a carriage or farm implement.
entries.example: The farmer checked the horse's harness before attaching the cart.

entries.definition: Any bird of the genus Falco, all of which are birds of prey.
entries.example: The falcon circled above the fields before diving.

entries.definition: A diurnal predatory bird of the family Accipitridae, smaller than an eagle.
entries.example: It is illegal to hunt hawks or other raptors in many parts of the world.

entries.definition: Any of several large carnivorous and carrion-eating birds in the family Accipitridae, having a powerful hooked bill and keen vision.
entries.example:
I, I go my own way
I swim against the stream
Forever I will fight the pοwers that be
The eagle flies alone

entries.definition: Any of various birds of prey of the order Strigiformes, families Strigidae and Tytonidae, that are primarily nocturnal and have forward-looking, binocular vision, limited eye movement, and good hearing.
entries.example: A group of owls is called a parliament.

entries.definition: To cause (food, drink etc.) to pass from the mouth into the stomach; to take into the stomach through the throat.
entries.example: What the liquor was I do not know, but it was not so strong but that I could swallow it in great gulps and found it less burning than my burning throat.

entries.definition: The house sparrow, Passer domesticus; a small bird with a short bill, and brown, white and gray feathers.
entries.example: Man progresses generally, not both legs at once like a sparrow, but by putting one leg forward first, and then the other.

entries.definition: One of several birds of the family Columbidae within the order Columbiformes.
entries.example: A pigeon landed on the station roof.

entries.definition: A bird, usually black, of the genus Corvus, having a strong conical beak, with projecting bristles; it has a harsh, croaking call.
entries.example: Gaslark in his splendour on the golden stairs saying adieu to those three captains and their matchless armament foredoomed to dogs and crows on Salapanta Hills.

entries.definition: Any of various species of large, long-necked waterfowl, of genus Cygnus (bird family: Anatidae), most of which have white plumage.
entries.example: A white swan glided across the lake.

entries.definition: Any of various grazing waterfowl of the family Anatidae, which have feathers and webbed feet and are capable of flying, swimming, and walking on land, and which are generally bigger than ducks.
entries.example: There is a flock of geese on the pond.

entries.definition: An adult male chicken or other male bird.
entries.example: The cock crowed at dawn.

entries.definition: Any mammal of the many rodent families (especially Muridae) that have a small body and a long tail.
entries.example: Near-synonyms: murine, murid, vole (all parasynonymous with this broad sense)

entries.definition: Any of the numerous members of several rodent families that usually have short limbs, a pointy snout, a long, hairless tail, and a body length greater than about 12 cm, or 5 inches.
entries.example: A rat had chewed through the bag of grain.

entries.definition: Any of the rodents of the family Sciuridae.
entries.example: tree squirrels

entries.definition: Any of several plant-eating mammals of the genus Lepus, similar to a rabbit, but larger and with longer ears.
entries.example: The hare has a reputation for exciting desire. Hare soup is credited with a particular aphrodisiac value.

entries.definition: Any of a class of small tailless amphibians of the order Anura that typically hop.
entries.example:
1 And the Lord spake vnto Moses, Goe vnto Pharaoh, and say vnto him; Thus sayeth the Lord, Let my people goe, that they may serue me.
2 And if thou refuse to let them goe, beholde, I will smite all thy borders with frogges.
3 And the riuer shall bring foorth frogges abundantly, which shall goe vp and come into thine house, and into thy bed-chamber, and vpon thy bed, and into the house of thy seruants, and vpon thy people, and into thine ouens, and into thy kneading troughes.
4 And the frogges shall come vp both on thee, and vpon thy people, and vpon all thy seruants.

entries.definition: British standard spelling of behavior.
entries.example: After all, it is undeniable that the B.R. standard coach scored highly in comparative trials with other European railway vehicles on the Continent a few years ago, so that B.R. civil engineers must share responsibility for any defects in its behaviour over here.

entries.definition: To cut into something by clamping the teeth.
entries.example: As soon as you bite that sandwich, you'll know how good it is.

entries.definition: A bump left on the skin after having been stung.
entries.example: Look at this nasty hornet sting: it's turned blue!

entries.definition: To make a short, loud, explosive noise with the vocal organs (said of animals, especially dogs).
entries.example: The neighbour's dog is always barking.

entries.definition: To make a loud, deep cry, especially from pain, anger, or other strong emotion.
entries.example: Sole on the barren ſands the ſuff'ring chief / Roar'd out for anguiſh, and indulg'd his grief.

entries.definition: An act of rubbing.
entries.example: Give that lamp a good rub and see if any genies come out.

entries.definition: To move slowly with the abdomen close to the ground.
entries.example: Lizards and snakes crept over the ground.

entries.definition: To move by dragging one's body along or close to a surface, like a worm or insect, or on one's hands and knees, like a human baby.
entries.example: Clutching my wounded side, I crawled back to the trench.

entries.definition: The natural place in which an organism lives.
entries.example: Road construction can destroy the habitat of rare species.
entries.usage: Typical combinations: natural habitat, habitat loss, protect a habitat.

entries.definition: A structure built by a bird as a place to incubate eggs and rear young.
entries.example: The robin built a nest under the eaves.

entries.definition: A structure, whether artificial or natural, for housing a swarm of honeybees.
entries.example: First, for thy Bees a quiet Station find, / And lodge 'em under Covert of the Wind: / For Winds, when homeward they return, will drive / The loaded Carriers from their Ev'ning Hive.

entries.definition: A single-room dwelling for a hermit.
entries.example: So, taking them apart into his cell, / He to that point fit speaches gan to frame […].

entries.definition: An enclosure made of spaced bars, normally to hold animals while providing some ventilation.
entries.example: We keep a bird in a cage.

entries.definition: Not changing significantly.
entries.example: The temperature remained stable throughout the experiment.

entries.definition: A building, often found on a farm, used for storage or keeping animals such as cattle.
entries.example: One day I was out in the barn and he drifted in. I was currying the horse and he set down on the wheelbarrow and begun to ask questions.

entries.definition: A thicket of bushes or other shrubbery, especially one planted as a fence between two portions of land, or to separate the parts of a garden.
entries.example: He trims the hedge once a week.

entries.definition: A structure that bars passage.
entries.example: The bus went through a railway barrier and was hit by a train.

entries.definition: A solid, more or less rigid object of metal or wood with a uniform cross-section smaller than its length.
entries.example: The window was protected by steel bars.

entries.definition: The science that deals with the form and structure of organic bodies; anatomical structure or organization.
entries.example: Animal anatomy is also called zootomy; vegetable anatomy, phytotomy; and human anatomy, anthropotomy.

entries.definition: A widespread disease that affects many humans in a population.
entries.example: At that time, the city [Christiania, now Oslo] was in the grip of a cholera epidemic, and victims were dying at the rate of 60 a day. Bradshaw contracted the disease, and died on September 6 [1853].

entries.definition: A theoretical unit of heredity of living organisms which may take several values and (in principle) predetermines a precise trait of an organism's form (phenotype), such as hair color.
entries.example: Near-synonym: cistron (often synonymous)

entries.definition: A microorganism or infectious agent that can cause disease.
entries.example: Washing your hands helps prevent germs from spreading.
entries.usage: Selected the common disease-related sense rather than the developing part of a seed.

entries.definition: Microscopic single-celled organisms, some of which cause disease while others are useful.
entries.example: Some bacteria help digest food in the human gut.

entries.definition: A submicroscopic, non-cellular structure that consists of a core of DNA or RNA surrounded by a protein coat, that requires a living host cell to replicate, and that sometimes causes disease in the host organism (such agents are often classed as nonliving infectious particles and less often as microorganisms).
entries.example: Viruses are the smallest and most simplified forms of life.

entries.definition: Any microorganism; (loosely, nonscientifically) especially, a harmful bacterium.
entries.example: We humans and other complex animals are full of microbes, gajillions of them. People have so many that microbe cells living in our bodies outnumber our own vastly.

entries.definition: The chemical processes that occur within a living organism in order to maintain life.
entries.example: The metabolisms of aerobic bacteria require oxygen

entries.definition: Any of numerous large, complex naturally-produced molecules composed of one or more long chains of amino acids, in which the amino acid groups are held together by peptide bonds.
entries.example: Proteins carry out the bulk of cellular functions, including relaying signals, providing structural support, and accelerating biochemical reactions.

entries.definition: Any of a specific group of organic compounds essential in small quantities for healthy human growth, metabolism, development, and body function. They are found in minute amounts in plant and animal foods or sometimes produced synthetically, and deficiencies of specific vitamins produce specific disorders.
entries.example: a food rich in vitamins

entries.definition: To extract a substance from blood, sap, or similar to produce and emit waste for excretion or for the fulfilling of a physiological function.
entries.example: Why one set of cells should secrete bile, another urea, and so on, we do not know.

entries.definition: To discharge material (including waste products) from a cell, body or system.
entries.example: Your open pores excrete sweat and dirt.

entries.definition: To eat quickly, greedily, hungrily, or ravenously.
entries.example: Once constituted, capital reproduces itself faster than output increases. The past devours the future.

entries.definition: A natural or inherent impulse or behaviour.
entries.example: Many animals fear fire by instinct.

entries.definition: Spontaneous, without requiring conscious thought.
entries.example: The intuitive response turned out to be correct.

entries.definition: A currently unrealized ability (with the most common adposition being to).
entries.example: Even from a young age it was clear that she had the potential to become a great musician.

entries.definition: The capacity of mind, especially to understand principles, truths, facts or meanings, acquire knowledge, and apply it to practice; the ability to comprehend and learn; the ability to process sentient experience to generate true beliefs with a justified degree of confidence.
entries.example: Not so, however, with Tarzan, the man-child. His life amidst the dangers of the jungle had taught him to meet emergencies with self-confidence, and his higher intelligence resulted in a quickness of mental action far beyond the powers of the apes.

entries.definition: In good working order.
entries.example: While we assume that phonological subsyllabic units are functional prior to reading skill, we have not ruled out a possible interaction with the writing system.

entries.definition: Having the faculty of sensation; pertaining to the senses.
entries.example: The sensitive faculty most part overrules reason, the soul is carried hoodwinked, and the understanding captive like a beast.

entries.definition: Capable of being flexed or bent without breaking; able to be turned or twisted without breaking.
entries.example: When the splitting wind Makes flexible the knees of knotted oaks.

entries.definition: Pertaining to the sense of hearing, the organs of hearing, or the science of sounds.
entries.example: The room's acoustic properties make speech easy to hear.

entries.definition: Of or relating to sight; visual.
entries.example: Strabismus is an optical defect.

entries.definition: Of a person, creature, group, or species, primarily active during the night.
entries.example: nocturnal birds

entries.definition: Inactive, sleeping, asleep, suspended.
entries.example: Grass goes dormant during the winter, waiting for spring before it grows again.

entries.definition: A state of minimum power consumption, inactivity and metabolic depression in some animals during winter.
entries.example: The bears are in hibernation.

entries.definition: A mark left by something that has passed along.
entries.example: Follow the track of the ship.

entries.definition: An act of tracing.
entries.example: Your cell phone company can put a trace on your line.

entries.definition: Happening by turns; one following the other in succession of time or place; first one and then the other (repeatedly).
entries.example: And bid alternate passions fall and rise

entries.definition: That which is or may be seized by animals to be devoured.
entries.example: The deer became prey to the lion.

entries.definition: Any animal or other organism that hunts and kills other nonplant organisms (their prey), primarily for food.
entries.example: Hives should be positioned, oriented and protected to avoid predators and ensure survival in the meliponary. A study (pers. obs.) of predators shows that the main culprits in a Malaysian meliponary are frogs and lizards.

entries.definition: A person harmed by an accident, crime or other event.
entries.example: The charity provides support for every victim of the flood.

entries.definition: One who has been captured or is otherwise confined.
entries.example:
I envy not in any moods
⁠The captive void of noble rage,
⁠The linnet born within the cage,
That never knew the summer woods: […]

entries.definition: Intended for defence; protective.
entries.example: a defensive perimeter

entries.definition: To experience; to pass through a phase.
entries.example: The project is undergoing great changes.

entries.definition: To undergo hardship.
entries.example: Many artists suffer before becoming famous.

entries.definition: More or most likely to be exposed to the chance of being attacked or harmed, either physically or emotionally.
entries.example: In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been turning over in my mind ever since. ‘Whenever you feel like criticizing any one,’ he told me, ‘just remember that all the people in this world haven’t had the advantages that you’ve had.’

entries.definition: Real being; existence.
entries.example: the human nature loseth its proper subsistence , and is assumed into the subsistence of the divine nature

entries.definition: to be; have existence; have being or reality
entries.example: Cognitive dissonance exists when a person possesses two cognitions, one of which is contradictory to the other

entries.definition: To kill or otherwise permanently eliminate all of (a population, often of pests or undesirables), usually intentionally.
entries.example: We'll use poison to exterminate the rats.

entries.definition: Under human control.
entries.example: The tame rabbit allowed the children to stroke it.

entries.definition: One who keeps (retains) something.
entries.example: Finders keepers; losers weepers.

entries.definition: A person who tends sheep, especially a grazing flock.
entries.example: It was April 22, 1831, and a young man was walking down Whitehall in the direction of Parliament Street. He wore shepherd's plaid trousers and the swallow-tail coat of the day, with a figured muslin cravat wound about his wide-spread collar.

entries.definition: Any of the collections of many millions or billions of stars, galactic dust, black holes, etc. existing as independent and coherent systems, of which there are billions in the known universe.
entries.example: The telescope captured a distant galaxy.

entries.definition: The universe regarded as a system with harmony and order.
entries.example: This doctrine [the nebular hypothesis] supposes all the material universe to have been once in a fluid or nebular condition, and that, by the operation of universal gravitation and the thousand other laws of nature, the nebular matter has been mainly aggregated into masses, and the existing cosmoi been developed.

entries.definition: All space, matter, energy, and time considered together.
entries.example: Galaxies are spread throughout the universe.
entries.usage: Common learner sense selected in place of an unsuitable or less useful source default.

entries.definition: Between the stars.
entries.example: It can take centuries for light to travel interstellar distances.

entries.definition: Living or growing on land rather than in water or another habitat.
entries.example: Most terrestrial mammals breathe air and move on land.
entries.usage: Selected the common adjective rather than the specialist plant noun.

entries.definition: Of, relating to, or located in the sky or outer space, where the Sun, Moon, planets, and stars are visible.
entries.example: [G]oe vvith ſpeede / To ſome forlorne and naked Hermytage, / Remote from all the pleaſurs of the vvorld: / There ſtay vntill the tvvelue Celeſtiall Signes / Haue brought about the annuall reckoning.

entries.definition: The study of the physical universe beyond the Earth's atmosphere, including the process of mapping locations and properties of the matter and radiation in the universe.
entries.example: The fact is, dark energy is the biggest mystery in science. It has driven a huge amount of research in the past decade, and was a key driver in last year’s “New Worlds, New Horizons” report from the National Academies of Science, which prioritized future astronomy and astrophysics projects.

entries.definition: Divination about human affairs or natural phenomena from the relative positions of celestial bodies.
entries.example: For if astronomy is the study of the movements of the heavens, then astrology is the study of the effects of those movements.

entries.definition: A member of the crew of a spaceship or other spacecraft that travels beyond Earth's atmosphere, or someone trained to serve that purpose.
entries.example: The astronaut checked her equipment before the spacewalk.

entries.definition: A small Solar System body consisting mainly of volatile ice, dust and particles of rock whose very eccentric solar orbit periodically brings it close enough to the Sun that the ice vaporises to form an atmosphere, or coma, which may be blown by the solar wind to produce a visible tail.
entries.example: And They made by the lifting of Their hands, each god according to his sign, the Bright One with the flaring tail to seek from the end of the Worlds to the end of them again, to return again after a hundred years. Man, when thou seest the comet, know that another seeketh besides thee nor ever findeth out.

entries.definition: A metallic or stony object or body that is the remains of a meteoroid.
entries.example: The Vestan, Lunar, and Martian meteorites are achondrites.

entries.definition: A hemispherical pit created by the impact of a meteorite or other object.
entries.example: The meteorite left a large crater in the desert.

entries.definition: Fine particles.
entries.example: There is so much dust released during the process of laying ballast that the trackside operator wears a full face mask with respirator.

entries.definition: The solid remains of a fire.
entries.example: The audience was more captivated by the growing ash at the end of his cigarette than by his words.

entries.definition: A paper or cardboard wrapper used to enclose small, flat items, especially letters, for mailing.
entries.example: Now we are liberal with our innermost secrets, spraying them into the public ether with a generosity our forebears could not have imagined. Where we once sent love letters in a sealed envelope, or stuck photographs of our children in a family album, now such private material is despatched to servers and clouds operated by people we don't know and will never meet.

entries.definition: A part of something that has been separated; a generally squat, thick, irregular piece of something, e.g. wood or stone.
entries.example: The statue broke into chunks.

entries.definition: A vehicle that travels through space.
entries.example: Today, Velcro is used for everything from keeping astronauts from floating off the floor of their spacecrafts to keeping artificial hearts in place, as well as the more mundane tasks of fastening clothing.

entries.definition: A manned vehicle that flies through space.
entries.example: The crew entered the spaceship before the launch.

entries.definition: Any of various medical instruments used to explore wounds, organs, etc.
entries.example: The surgeon used a probe to examine the wound.

entries.definition: A self-contained component of a system, often interchangeable, which has a well-defined interface to the other components.
entries.example: A friend who’s spent decades as an auto mechanic recently confided that he’s grateful to be nearing retirement. “These Teslas,” he told me, “they’re not even cars anymore – they’re computers on wheels. When something goes wrong, you don’t fix it; you just replace entire modules.” What was once a craft that any dedicated person could learn has become an exercise in supervised dependency.

entries.definition: The process of propelling, driving, or pushing, typically forward or onward; a propulsive force or impulse.
entries.example: The boat uses an electric motor for propulsion.

entries.definition: A pressing; a force applied to a surface.
entries.example: Apply pressure to the wound to stop the bleeding.

entries.definition: The branch of mechanics that is concerned with the effects of forces on the motion of objects.
entries.example: The course in dynamics explains why a moving object accelerates when a force acts on it.

entries.definition: A change whereby something goes from one place to another; a state of progression from one place to another; a change of position with respect to time.
entries.example: This is the great wheel to which the clock owes its motion.

entries.definition: An opening through which gases, especially air, can pass.
entries.example: the vent of a cask; the vent of a mould

entries.definition: The caudal appendage of an animal that is attached to their posterior and near the anus or cloaca.
entries.example: Most primates have a tail and fangs.

entries.definition: A bend, such as in a road.
entries.example: You should slow down when approaching a curve.

entries.definition: The process of exploring.
entries.example: By this time, largely inspired by The Railway Magazine, I had begun to spread my wings, and had started on a long career of railway exploration.

entries.definition: A military journey; an enterprise against some enemy or into enemy territory.
entries.example: Once established in their capital at Nanking, occupied March, 1853, and renamed “Heavenly Capital” (T’ien-ching), the Taipings sent out an expedition to take Peking which again made striking gains initially, but was eventually slowed, isolated, and defeated.

entries.definition: A flight past a celestial object in order to make observations.
entries.example: The upcoming flyby of Halley's comet is expected to provide new information on the nature of the comet.

entries.definition: A place where stars, planets and other celestial bodies are observed, usually through a telescope; also place for observing meteorological or other natural phenomena.
entries.example: The corporation of Harvard University have passed a vote closing the observatory in Cambridge to the public on Saturday evenings.

entries.definition: A monocular optical instrument that magnifies distant objects, especially in astronomy.
entries.example: It needs a scientific telescope, it needs to be reinterpreted and artificially brought near us, before we can so much as know that it was a Sun.

entries.definition: An exciting or extraordinary scene, exhibition, performance etc.
entries.example: The horse race was a thrilling spectacle.

entries.definition: The curved path of one object around a point or another body.
entries.example: The satellite remains in orbit around Earth.

entries.definition: The great circle on the celestial sphere that is the mean apparent path of the sun as viewed from the earth.
entries.example: The Sun appears to move along the ecliptic over the course of a year.

entries.definition: Any straight line between two points on the circumference of a circle that passes through the center of the circle; a chord that passes through the center of the circle.
entries.example: Draw a diameter through the centre of the circle.

entries.definition: The long bone in the forearm, on the side of the thumb.
entries.example: It is also obvious, and proved by experiment, that the rotatory motions observed in the hand proceed from the rotatory motions of the radius.

entries.definition: Physical matter; material.
entries.example: Study gives strength to the mind; conversation, grace: the first apt to give stiffness, the other suppleness: one gives substance and form to the statue, the other polishes it.

entries.definition: The parts or materials that make up something.
entries.example: The scientist analysed the composition of the soil.

entries.definition: An enclosure within which workers, prisoners, or soldiers are confined.
entries.example: Soldiers checked every vehicle entering the compound.

entries.definition: The mineralized remains of an animal or plant.
entries.example: With the permission of the Keeper of the fossil collection, therefore, the specimen was subjected to a further careful removal of the matrix in the requisite directions.

entries.definition: A smaller selection used to represent or examine a larger whole.
entries.example: The researchers interviewed a representative sample of residents.
entries.usage: Typical combinations: representative sample, sample size, random sample.

entries.definition: An individual instance that represents a class; an example.
entries.example: early specimens of the art of Picasso

entries.definition: A very small piece of matter, a fragment; especially, the smallest possible part of something.
entries.example: Be content with the knowledge that, ere the voyage had ended, both she and I were desperately and unreasoningly in love with one another. Heaven knows that I can make the admission now without one particle of vanity.

entries.definition: The smallest particle of a specific element or compound that retains the chemical properties of that element or compound; two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.
entries.example: Hydrogen chloride is a diatomic molecule, consisting of a hydrogen atom and a chlorine atom.

entries.definition: The smallest possible amount of matter which still retains its identity as a chemical element, now known to consist of a nucleus surrounded by electrons.
entries.example: Oxygen levels on Earth skyrocketed 2.4 billion years ago, when cyanobacteria evolved photosynthesis: the ability to convert water and carbon dioxide into carbohydrates and waste oxygen using solar energy. The evolutionary precursor of photosynthesis is still under debate, and a new study sheds light. The critical component of the photosynthetic system is the water-oxidizing complex, made up of manganese atoms and a calcium atom.

entries.definition: An atom or group of atoms bearing an electrical charge, such as the sodium and chlorine atoms in a salt solution.
entries.example: A sodium ion carries a positive electrical charge.

entries.definition: The subatomic particle having a negative charge and orbiting the nucleus; the flow of electrons in a conductor constitutes electricity.
entries.example: An electron carries a negative electric charge.

entries.definition: The total amount of something; quantity.
entries.example: The reader will perhaps be curious to know the quantum of this present, but we cannot satisfy his curiosity.

entries.definition: Something which is related to, or in some way affects, a fact or event.
entries.example: The report should focus on to the current circumstances of the organisation, to help us find a way to grow in the future.

entries.definition: A substance that is flowing, and keeping no shape, such as water; a substance of which the molecules, while not tending to separate from one another like those of a gas, readily change their relative position, and which therefore retains no definite shape, except that determined by the containing receptacle; an inelastic fluid.
entries.example: A liquid can freeze to become a solid or evaporate into a gas.

entries.definition: Any substance which can flow with relative ease, tends to assume the shape of its container, and obeys Bernoulli's principle; a liquid, gas or plasma.
entries.example: An extreme version of vorticity is a vortex. The vortex is a spinning, cyclonic mass of fluid, which can be observed in the rotation of water going down a drain, as well as in smoke rings, tornados and hurricanes.

entries.definition: That can be picked up or held, having a texture, and usually firm. Unlike a liquid, gas or plasma.
entries.example: Almost all metals are solid at room temperature.

entries.definition: Combine separate ideas or materials into a coherent whole.
entries.example: The report synthesises evidence from several studies.

entries.definition: The act of assembling a group or structure.
entries.example: Some cloud formation was confirmed and rainfall was observed over some islands.

entries.definition: A process by which a task is completed; a way of doing something (followed by the adposition of, to or for before the purpose of the process).
entries.example: If one method doesn't work, you should ask a friend to help you.

entries.definition: A range; a continuous, infinite, one-dimensional set, possibly bounded by extremes.
entries.example: Near-synonyms: sliding scale, continuum

entries.definition: A single aspect of a given thing.
entries.example: This film can be enjoyed on many dimensions - the script is great, the acting is realistic, and the special effects will simply take you aback.

entries.definition: The rate of occurrence of anything; the relationship between incidence and time period.
entries.example: With growing confidence, the Viking’s raids increased in frequency.

entries.definition: A sequence of states representing an encoded message in a communication channel.
entries.example: The receiver converts the radio signal into sound.

entries.definition: An appendage used for sensing on the head of an insect, crab, or other animal.
entries.example: The overall shape of most insect antennae is elongate and cylindrical, although elaborations into plumose, lamellate, or pectinate forms have arisen many times in different insect lineages.

entries.definition: The act of moving or revolving around, or as in a circle or orbit; a revolution
entries.example: After 27 days the moon has made one circuit among the stars, moving from west to east. But in those 27 days the sun has likewise moved eastwardly, about 27 degrees. The moon, then, has to make one circuit and a little more in order to be again in the line joining the earth and sun, in order to be again 'new.'

entries.definition: The turning or bending of any wave, such as a light or sound wave, when it passes from one medium into another of different optical density.
entries.example: Refraction makes the straw appear bent in a glass of water.

entries.definition: Of electromagnetic radiation beyond (higher in frequency than) light visible to the human eye; radiation with wavelengths from 380 to 10 nanometres.
